title: Addition & Subtraction
blurb: Column addition and subtraction with regrouping inside 10 000, mental strategies, missing-number fact families, and one- and two-step word problems.

lessons.title: Column Addition
lessons.concreteComparison: Counting money after a market day: you sort the togrog notes into piles — thousands, hundreds, tens, ones — and count each pile on its own. Whenever ten small notes stack up, you swap them for one bigger note. Column addition is exactly that sorting: line the places up, add each pile, and trade every ten upward.
lessons.objective: Add three- and four-digit numbers in columns — lining up places, adding from the ones, carrying past nine — and check every sum by adding the other way.
concept: **Places line up from the right.** Ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. A digit's column IS its value — slide $47$ one place left and it silently becomes $470$.

**Add from the ones and trade every ten.** $8 + 7 = 15$ ones is too many for one column: five stay, and ten of them trade for $1$ ten that moves next door. The carry is real value on the move — and when you add TWO numbers it is always exactly $1$. (Stack three or more numbers in a column and a bigger carry can appear: $9 + 9 + 9 = 27$ carries a $2$.)

**Check by adding the other way.** $358 + 467$ and $467 + 358$ walk different roads to the SAME total. Re-adding in the other order is the sum's receipt: if the two answers disagree, a carry slipped somewhere.
lessons.keyIdea: Line up the places, add from the right, and trade every ten upward — then add the other way and make the total repeat.

facts.title: Ten of these make one of those
facts.explanation: Carrying is trading: ten in one column become one in the next.

facts.title: The other-way check
facts.explanation: Order never changes a sum — add the other way and the total must repeat.

workedExamples.statement: Add $358 + 467$ in columns, then check by adding the other way.
workedExamples.note: Ones first; every ten trades up.
workedExamples.solution: Ones: $8 + 7 = 15$ — write $5$, carry $1$. Tens: $5 + 6 + 1 = 12$ — write $2$, carry $1$. Hundreds: $3 + 4 + 1 = 8$. Total $825$. Other way: $467 + 358 = 825$ ✓.

workedExamples.note: The hundreds outgrow one digit — the total crosses 1000.
workedExamples.solution: Ones: $5 + 9 = 14$. Tens: $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$. Hundreds: $7 + 6 + 1 = 14$ — fourteen hundreds are $1$ thousand $4$ hundreds. Total $1\,434$; other way $649 + 785 = 1\,434$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Lining numbers up on the left — writing the 4 of 47 under the 3 of 385.
commonMistakes.correction: Places line up from the RIGHT: ones under ones, tens under tens. 47 + 385 is 432; left-aligned, the 47 acts as 470 and the sum silently becomes 855.

commonMistakes.text: Writing a two-digit column total straight down — a 15 squeezed into the ones column.
commonMistakes.correction: 15 ones are 1 ten and 5 ones: write the 5, carry the 1 into the tens column. The carry is real value, not decoration.

tryIt.statement: Add $276 + 358$ and check it the other way.

steps.title: Line up, add from the right, trade
beats: Write the numbers so PLACES line up — ones under ones, tens under tens, hundreds under hundreds. In $358 + 467$, the $8$ and the $7$ share the ones column.
Add from the RIGHT. Ones first: $8 + 7 = 15$ — too many for one column. Ten of those ones trade for ONE ten: write $5$, carry $1$ into the tens.
The carry is real value, not decoration. Tens: $5 + 6 + 1 = 12$ — write $2$, carry $1$ again. Hundreds: $3 + 4 + 1 = 8$. Total: $825$.

steps.title: Carrying past nine
steps.intro: Ones first, and every ten trades up.

steps: Ones: $9 + 6 = 15$ — write $5$, carry $1$. Tens: $2 + 8 + 1 = 11$ — write $1$, carry $1$.

steps.title: Carry it over
steps.intro: Ones first; trade every ten upward.

problems.explanation: Ones $7 + 5 = 12$ (write $2$, carry $1$); tens $4 + 8 + 1 = 13$; hundreds $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$: $632$. Dropping the carries gives $522$ — the no-trade trap.
Ones $8 + 3 = 11$ (write $1$, carry $1$); tens $0 + 9 + 1 = 10$ (write $0$, carry $1$); hundreds $5 + 2 + 1 = 8$: $801$. Forgetting the ones carry leaves $791$.
Ones $4 + 7 = 11$; tens $3 + 8 + 1 = 12$; hundreds $6 + 1 + 1 = 8$: $821$. Missing the tens carry gives $721$.

steps.title: Columns are places
steps.prompt: To add $47 + 385$, Dorj lines the numbers up on the LEFT, so the $4$ of $47$ sits under the $3$ of $385$. What really happens?
options: the $47$ acts as $470$, and the sum comes out $855$ instead of $432$
nothing — lining up on the left works just as well
steps.explanation: Columns are PLACES. Slid one place left, the $4$ of $47$ sits in the tens — the addition quietly computes $470 + 385 = 855$. Lined up from the right it is $47 + 385 = 432$.

steps.title: The carry that stays a 1
steps.body: When you add TWO numbers, however long they get, one column can hold at most $9 + 9 = 18$, plus an incoming carry: $19$ at the very most. That is one ten and nine ones — so the number you carry is always exactly $1$, never more. The scariest-looking two-number column addition still moves only a quiet little $1$. Stack THREE or more numbers, though, and the carry can grow — $9 + 9 + 9 = 27$ writes $7$ and carries $2$.

steps.title: Into the thousands — and the other-way check
beats: Two three-digit numbers can outgrow three digits: $785 + 649$ — ones $5 + 9 = 14$, tens $8 + 4 + 1 = 13$, hundreds $7 + 6 + 1 = 14$. Fourteen hundreds are $1$ thousand $4$ hundreds: $1\,434$.

That is as big as it gets for two three-digit numbers: even $999 + 999 = 1\,998$, so the answer never needs more than one extra digit. And nothing changes when the numbers themselves are four digits — $1\,748 + 2\,596$ simply adds one more column, the thousands.

Now the through-line of this whole topic: one fact can be read two ways. Check every sum by adding the OTHER way — $649 + 785$ must land on the same $1\,434$. If the two reads disagree, one of them slipped.

steps.title: Crossing 1000 — and four digits
steps.intro: Add both ways; the total must repeat.

examples.prompt: Add $785 + 649$, then check by adding the other way.
steps: Other way: $649 + 785 = 1\,434$ — same total, sum confirmed.

examples.prompt: Add $1\,748 + 2\,596$ — four digits, one more column.
steps: Ones $8 + 6 = 14$ (write $4$, carry $1$); tens $4 + 9 + 1 = 14$ (write $4$, carry $1$); hundreds $7 + 5 + 1 = 13$ (write $3$, carry $1$).
Thousands are just the next column along: $1 + 2 + 1 = 4$. Total $4\,344$; other way $2\,596 + 1\,748 = 4\,344$ ✓.

steps.title: Past a thousand
steps.intro: Four-digit totals, checked the other way.

problems.explanation: Ones $6 + 9 = 15$; tens $5 + 7 + 1 = 13$; hundreds $8 + 3 + 1 = 12$: $1\,235$. $1\,125$ dropped the carries; $477$ subtracted instead of adding ($856 - 379 = 477$, since $477 + 379 = 856$).
Ones $4 + 7 = 11$; tens $0 + 1 + 1 = 2$; hundreds $6 + 5 = 11$ — eleven hundreds are one thousand one hundred: $1\,121$. $1\,111$ lost the ones carry; $121$ lost the thousand.

problems.prompt: You computed $358 + 467 = 825$. Which check adds the SAME two numbers in the other order?
options: compute $358 + 467$ once more, the same way
problems.explanation: Swapping the order re-walks the sum by a different road: $467 + 358 = 825$ ✓. Adding $825 + 467$ climbs to $1\,292$ — a sum can never shrink back to $358$. Re-adding the same way just repeats any slip.

Four digits, four columns: ones $5 + 6 = 11$; tens $7 + 4 + 1 = 12$; hundreds $3 + 8 + 1 = 12$; thousands $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$: $4\,221$, and the other way $1\,846 + 2\,375 = 4\,221$ ✓. $4\,211$ dropped the ones carry.

steps.title: The ceiling
steps.prompt: The LARGEST total two three-digit numbers can make is:
steps.explanation: $999 + 999 = 1\,998$ — so the sum of two three-digit numbers never needs more than four digits, and when it does grow a digit, that digit is always $1$: $1\,998 < 2\,000$.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Line up places from the right: ones under ones, tens under tens.
Add from the ones; ten in any column trades for one in the next.
Adding TWO numbers, the carry is always exactly 1 — a column holds at most 9 + 9 + 1 = 19. (Stack three or more and a bigger carry can appear.)
Two three-digit numbers can reach four digits, never five.
Check every sum by adding the other way — the total must repeat.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Say the trade out loud each time it happens — 'fifteen ones: five stay, one ten moves' — and finish every sum with the other-way check.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Columns, carries, and the other-way check.

problems.explanation: Ones $3 + 9 = 12$; tens $6 + 4 + 1 = 11$; hundreds $2 + 3 + 1 = 6$: $612$. $602$ lost the ones carry.
Ones $8 + 6 = 14$; tens $7 + 4 + 1 = 12$; hundreds $5 + 2 + 1 = 8$: $824$. $814$ dropped the ones carry into the tens.

Every column trades: ones $5 + 5 = 10$, tens $4 + 5 + 1 = 10$, hundreds $7 + 2 + 1 = 10$ — a clean thousand. $990$ carried nothing — it wrote the $0$ from $5 + 5$, then added $4 + 5 = 9$ and $7 + 2 = 9$ with no trades at all.

problems.prompt: A herder counts $486$ sheep and $375$ goats. How many animals altogether?
problems.explanation: Altogether joins the flocks: $486 + 375 = 861$, and the other-way check $375 + 486 = 861$ agrees. $851$ lost the ones carry.

steps.title: You've finished "Column Addition"
steps.body: Line up, add from the right, trade every ten — and let the other-way check sign each answer. Next the machine runs in reverse: column subtraction, where every answer signs its receipt with the addition you just mastered.

lessons.title: Column Subtraction
lessons.concreteComparison: You owe a friend eight one-togrog coins but your pocket holds only four — so you break one ten-togrog coin into ten ones. Nothing gained, nothing lost: your money just changed outfits. Column subtraction regroups the same way — and afterwards you add your answer back, to prove nothing leaked.
lessons.objective: Subtract three- and four-digit numbers with regrouping — including tops with zeros like $503 - 168$ and $3\,005 - 1\,428$ — and prove every answer with the add-back check.
concept: **The top number is the one being cut.** $634 - 278$ asks what is LEFT of $634$ — so when a top digit runs short ($4$ ones facing $8$), you may not flip the column around. Open a ten instead: $634$ becomes $6$ hundreds, $2$ tens, $14$ ones — same value, readier outfit.

**Zeros pass the borrow along.** In $503 - 168$ the tens hold nothing to lend, so knock one door further: a hundred opens into ten tens, THEN a ten opens into ten ones — $503 = 400 + 90 + 13$. Check the outfit before subtracting: it must still total $503$.

**The add-back receipt, every time.** Subtraction and addition are one fact read two ways: if $634 - 278 = 356$, then $356 + 278$ must rebuild $634$. Add the answer back every single time — a wrong answer fails its receipt on the spot.
lessons.keyIdea: When the top digit runs short, open the next place — and prove every difference by adding it back: answer plus what you took away must rebuild what you started with.

facts.title: Open a ten when the top runs short
facts.explanation: Same number, new outfit — now the ones column can pay.

facts.title: The add-back receipt
facts.explanation: Every subtraction is checked by the addition that undoes it.

workedExamples.note: Two tops run short — open a ten, then a hundred.
The tens are zero — the borrow travels through them.
workedExamples.solution: The tens hold nothing to lend, so open a hundred into ten tens, then a ten into ten ones: $503 = 400 + 90 + 13$. Now subtract: $13 - 8 = 5$, $9 - 6 = 3$, $4 - 1 = 3$ — answer $335$. Receipt: $335 + 168 = 503$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Flipping a column to bigger-minus-smaller — for 634 − 278 computing 8 − 4 in the ones.
commonMistakes.correction: The TOP number is the one being cut. If its digit is smaller, regroup — open a ten. Flip-work gives 444 here, and the receipt exposes it: 444 + 278 = 722, not 634.

commonMistakes.text: Jumping over a zero when borrowing — in 503 − 168, taking ones straight from the hundreds and leaving the tens untouched.
commonMistakes.correction: Go through the zero door by door: 5 hundreds become 4 hundreds and 10 tens; one of those tens becomes 10 ones. Check it: 503 = 400 + 90 + 13 — then subtract.

tryIt.statement: Compute $725 - 468$, then prove it with the add-back check.

steps.title: Open a ten, then sign the receipt
beats: Subtract from the right, and remember which number is being cut: $634 - 278$ asks what is left of $634$. Ones first: $4 - 8$ cannot happen — the top ran short.
Do not flip the column. REGROUP: open one of the $3$ tens into $10$ ones — now $634$ wears $6$ hundreds, $2$ tens, $14$ ones, and $14 - 8 = 6$ works fine.
Tens next: $2 < 7$, so a hundred opens — $12 - 7 = 5$; hundreds $5 - 2 = 3$. Answer $356$ — and the receipt seals it: $356 + 278 = 634$ ✓.

steps.title: Opening tens
steps.intro: The top runs short? Open the next place — then receipt.

steps: Ones: $14 - 8 = 6$ (a ten opened). Tens: $12 - 7 = 5$ (a hundred opened).

steps.title: Regroup and receipt
steps.intro: Open the place, subtract, add it back.

problems.explanation: Ones $11 - 6 = 5$; tens $13 - 5 = 8$; hundreds $6 - 3 = 3$: $385$, receipted by $385 + 356 = 741$ ✓. $415$ flipped columns to bigger-minus-smaller; $495$ forgot to reduce after lending.
Ones $13 - 9 = 4$; tens $11 - 8 = 3$; hundreds $5 - 1 = 4$: $434$, and $434 + 189 = 623$ ✓. $566$ flipped every column.
Ones $17 - 8 = 9$; tens $10 - 2 = 8$; hundreds $8 - 5 = 3$: $389$, and $389 + 528 = 917$ ✓. $499$ subtracted without ever reducing a lender.

steps.title: The receipt catches the flip
steps.prompt: For $634 - 278$, Suvdaa works each column as bigger digit minus smaller and gets $444$. What does the add-back check say?
options: $444 + 278 = 722$, not $634$ — the receipt fails, so $444$ is wrong
the add-back check cannot catch this kind of slip
steps.explanation: The top number is the one being cut — flipping a column answers a different question. The receipt exposes it: $444 + 278 = 722$, not $634$. The true answer $356$ passes: $356 + 278 = 634$ ✓.

steps.title: Cashiers count up
steps.body: Watch change being made at a market stall: pay $1\,000$ togrog for something costing $640$, and many sellers count UPWARD — six hundred forty, six hundred fifty, seven hundred, one thousand — dropping coins into your hand as they go. They are running the add-back check with real money: $640 + 360 = 1\,000$, so the change is $360$.

steps.title: Zeros on top
beats: $503 - 168$: the ones run short, but the tens have NOTHING to lend. Knock on the next door: open a hundred into ten tens first.
Now a ten can open into ten ones: $503$ wears $4$ hundreds, $9$ tens, $13$ ones. Pause and check the outfit: $400 + 90 + 13 = 503$ — nothing leaked.
Subtract: $13 - 8 = 5$, $9 - 6 = 3$, $4 - 1 = 3$ — answer $335$. Receipt: $335 + 168 = 503$ ✓. Zeros just pass the borrow along; the receipt signs exactly as before.

steps.title: Borrowing through zero
steps.intro: Open the hundred, then the ten — check the outfit, then subtract.

steps: The tens and hundreds are zero, so the borrow walks all the way to the thousands: $3\,005 = 2\,000 + 900 + 90 + 15$ (check: still $3\,005$).

steps.title: Through the zero
steps.intro: The borrow travels door to door; the receipt still signs.

problems.explanation: $605 = 500 + 90 + 15$; subtract: $367$, receipted by $367 + 238 = 605$ ✓. $433$ flipped columns; $467$ forgot to reduce the hundreds.
$1\,000 = 900 + 90 + 10$ — three doors open in a row. Subtract: $326$, receipted by $326 + 674 = 1\,000$ ✓.

$4\,006 = 3\,000 + 900 + 90 + 16$ — the borrow walks through both zeros. Subtract: $2\,127$, receipted by $2\,127 + 1\,879 = 4\,006$ ✓. $3\,873$ flipped every column; $3\,127$ forgot to reduce the thousands after lending.

steps.title: Check the outfit
steps.explanation: Only the first still totals $503$: $400 + 90 + 13 = 503$ ✓. The second claims $500 + 13 = 513$, the third only $413$ — but regrouping must never change the number, only its outfit.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The top number is the one being cut — never flip a column.
Top digit short? Open a ten; zeros pass the borrow to the next door.
Check every regroup: the new outfit must total the same number.
The add-back receipt, every time: difference + subtracted = start.
A flipped or leaky answer fails its receipt instantly.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: No subtraction is finished until its receipt is signed: add your answer to the number you took away, and watch the starting number reappear.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Regrouping, zeros, and a receipt for every answer.

problems.explanation: Ones $12 - 7 = 5$; tens $13 - 6 = 7$; hundreds $4 - 2 = 2$: $275$, and $275 + 267 = 542$ ✓. $325$ flipped the columns.
Through the zero: $806 = 700 + 90 + 16$; subtract to $447$, receipted by $447 + 359 = 806$ ✓.
$903 = 800 + 90 + 13$; subtract to $446$, and $446 + 457 = 903$ ✓. $554$ flipped every column.

problems.prompt: A ger camp steamed $500$ buuz for a feast; $268$ were eaten. How many are left?
problems.explanation: What is left is a subtraction: $500 - 268 = 232$, receipted by $232 + 268 = 500$ ✓. $368$ flipped the columns.

steps.title: You've finished "Column Subtraction"
steps.body: Regroup when the top runs short, walk borrows through zeros, and let every difference sign its add-back receipt. Next: leaving the columns behind — the mental moves that make many of these sums faster than paper.

lessons.title: Mental Strategies
lessons.concreteComparison: To pay $99$ togrog you do not count out ninety-nine coins — you hand over a hundred and take one back. Mental arithmetic works the same way: slide the numbers to a round, friendly place, do the easy sum there, and settle the small difference after. The answer never changes; only the road gets smoother.
lessons.objective: Add and subtract in your head using make-ten, near-doubles, and compensation — moving amounts between numbers and giving back overshoots — with a number-line picture of every jump.
concept: **Make a ten: jump to round ground.** $48 + 27$: move $2$ out of the $27$ to fill $48$ up to $50$, then jump the easy $25$: $50 + 25 = 75$. What one number gains, the other must lose — the total never moves.
**Near-doubles ride a known fact.** $47 + 48$ sits next to a double you already own: $47 + 47 = 94$, so one more makes $95$. Spot neighbours and let the double carry the load.

**Compensation overshoots on purpose.** Adding $99$ is awkward; adding $100$ is instant: $356 + 100 = 456$, then give the extra $1$ back — $455$. Subtracting works too: for $725 - 98$, jump back the round $100$ — $725 - 100 = 625$ took $2$ too many, so hand $2$ back: $627$.
lessons.keyIdea: Slide the sum to round ground — fill tens, lean on doubles, overshoot to hundreds — and always settle the difference you moved.

facts.title: Make a ten
facts.explanation: The 2 that fills 48 to 50 comes out of the 27 — totals never change when amounts just move.

facts.title: Compensation
facts.explanation: Overshoot to the round hundred, then give the extra 1 back.

workedExamples.statement: Compute $48 + 27$ in your head with the make-ten strategy.
workedExamples.note: Fill 48 up to the next round ten first.
workedExamples.solution: Take $2$ from the $27$: $48 + 2 = 50$, and $25$ remains to add (because $2 + 25 = 27$). Then $50 + 25 = 75$. One tidy jump to round ground, one easy jump after.
Overshoot: $356 + 100 = 456$. Give the extra $1$ back: $456 - 1 = 455$ (and $455 + 1 = 456$ confirms the settle). So $356 + 99 = 455$.

commonMistakes.text: Moving an amount without taking it from anywhere — 48 + 27 computed as 50 + 27.
commonMistakes.correction: The 2 that filled 48 up to 50 came OUT of the 27: what remains is 25, and 50 + 25 = 75. What one number gains, the other must lose.

commonMistakes.text: Settling the wrong way after subtracting — 725 − 98 finished as 625 − 2.
commonMistakes.correction: Subtracting 100 took away 2 TOO MANY, so give the 2 back: 625 + 2 = 627. The receipt confirms it: 627 + 98 = 725.

tryIt.statement: Compute $725 - 98$ with compensation, and receipt the answer.
tryIt.solution: $725 - 100 = 625$ — that took $2$ too many, so give them back: $625 + 2 = 627$. Receipt: $627 + 98 = 725$ ✓.

steps.title: Fill the ten, lean on a double
beats: See $48 + 27$ on the number line: standing at $48$, the next round ten is $50$ — just $2$ away. Take that $2$ out of the $27$ and jump to round ground.
From $50$ the rest is easy: $25$ remains (because $2 + 25 = 27$), and $50 + 25 = 75$. Two friendly jumps instead of one awkward one.
Near-doubles pull the same trick with a fact you own: $47 + 48$ leans on $47 + 47 = 94$ — one more makes $95$. Move amounts, lean on rounds and doubles; the total never changes.

steps.title: Jumps to round ground
steps.intro: Fill the ten; let a double do the lifting.

steps.title: Slide and jump
steps.intro: Move an amount, then jump round-to-round.

problems.explanation: Fill $48$ to $50$ with $2$ from the $36$ — $34$ remains ($34 + 2 = 36$): $50 + 34 = 84$. Choosing $86$ counts the moved $2$ twice ($50 + 36$).
Take $5$ from the $29$: $65 + 5 = 70$, then $70 + 24 = 94$. Answering $95$ jumps $65 + 30$ and never gives the extra $1$ back.
Double: $25 + 25 = 50$; one more: $51$. $50$ is the bare double — the extra $1$ still wants in.

steps.title: Pick the move
steps.prompt: Which move computes $57 + 36$ by MAKING A TEN?
steps.explanation: The next round ten above $57$ is $60$ — exactly $3$ away, and the $3$ comes out of the $36$: $60 + 33 = 93$. Moving $6$ lands on $63$ — the total survives, but there is no round ground to stand on. Adding only the tens abandons $13$.

steps.title: Fingers named the digits
steps.body: The Latin word for finger is digitus — and that is exactly why the symbols $0$ to $9$ are called DIGITS. People counted on ten fingers, numbers settled into a ten-based system, and the fingers' own name stuck to the figures. Every make-ten jump lands on the base your hands built.

steps.title: Overshoot and settle
beats: Compensation on the line: to add $99$, overshoot with one big jump of $100$ — $356 + 100 = 456$ — then step $1$ back: $455$. Big jump, small settle.
Subtraction compensates too, but settle the OTHER way: $725 - 98$ — jump back $100$ to $625$; that removed $2$ too many, so walk $2$ forward: $627$.
The receipt still rules the lesson: $627 + 98 = 725$ ✓. Mental shortcuts change the road, never the destination — and they never escape their receipts.

steps.title: Round jump first
steps.intro: Overshoot to the round number; settle the difference after.

steps.title: Settle the difference
steps.intro: Which way does the settle go? Say it before you jump.

problems.explanation: $534 + 100 = 634$, then give the $2$ back: $632$ ($632 + 2 = 634$ confirms). Stopping at $634$ keeps the borrowed $2$.
$500 - 200 = 300$ took $1$ too many — give it back: $301$, receipted by $301 + 199 = 500$ ✓. $299$ settled the wrong way.
$276 + 100 = 376$, give $1$ back: $375$ ($375 + 1 = 376$). $376$ keeps the borrowed $1$; $275$ subtracted $1$ from $276$ and never added the hundred.

steps.title: Settle the right way
steps.prompt: For $700 - 298$, Naran computes $700 - 300 = 400$, then takes $2$ MORE off and answers $398$. The truth:
options: taking $300$ removed $2$ too many — give them back: $402$
$398$ is right — overshoots always subtract again
steps.explanation: Removing $300$ removes MORE than $298$, so the running answer is $2$ too small: settle forward, $400 + 2 = 402$. Receipt: $402 + 298 = 700$ ✓. Settling backward doubles the error instead of fixing it.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Make a ten: move just enough to reach round ground — the moved amount comes OUT of the other number.
Near-doubles: compute the double you know, then adjust by 1.
Compensation: overshoot to a round number, then settle — back after adding too much, forward after subtracting too much.
Mental shortcuts change the road, never the total — receipts still apply.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Before each one, say the move you chose — fill the ten, lean on a double, or overshoot and settle. Naming the road is half the trip.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: All three tools; pick the smoothest road.

problems.explanation: Fill $38$ to $40$ with $2$ from the $45$ — $43$ remains ($43 + 2 = 45$): $40 + 43 = 83$. $85$ counts the moved $2$ twice.
Near-double: $75 + 75 = 150$, one more: $151$. $150$ is the bare double.
$632 - 100 = 532$, give the $2$ back: $534$, receipted by $534 + 98 = 632$ ✓. $530$ settled the wrong way; $532$ never settled.
Overshoot twice: $1\,000 + 1\,000 = 2\,000$, then give back $1 + 1 = 2$: $1\,998$ — the same ceiling column addition met. $2\,000$ keeps the borrowed $2$.

steps.title: You've finished "Mental Strategies"
steps.body: Fill the ten, lean on a double, overshoot and settle — three roads to the same honest total. Next: equations with a missing number, where the receipt idea stops checking answers and starts FINDING them.

lessons.title: Missing Numbers
lessons.concreteComparison: Three numbers — $53$, $38$ and their whole $91$ — live like a small family in one ger: know any two and you know the third. Cover the $91$: the parts rebuild it. Cover the $53$: the whole gives it back as $91 - 38$. Three numbers, four facts, and no strangers allowed in.
lessons.objective: Read a fact family as four faces of one fact, and solve box equations like $\square + 38 = 91$ with the inverse operation — always checking by substitution.
concept: **Three numbers, four facts.** $53$, $38$ and $91$ hold together: $53 + 38 = 91$, $38 + 53 = 91$, $91 - 38 = 53$, $91 - 53 = 38$. Two additions, two subtractions — one triangle of numbers wearing four outfits.

**The inverse opens the box.** $\square + 38 = 91$ hides a family member. Addition put the $38$ in; subtraction takes it out: $\square = 91 - 38 = 53$. And when the box was cut — $\square - 47 = 129$ — addition restores it: $\square = 129 + 47 = 176$.

**Substitution is the receipt.** An answer for the box is only an OFFER until you put it back in: $53 + 38 = 91$ ✓ — now it is a fact. Substitute every time; a wrong box fails its own equation on the spot.
lessons.keyIdea: A fact family is one fact wearing four outfits — so a box equation is solved by the family member that undoes it, and proved by substitution.

facts.title: One family, four facts
facts.explanation: The whole stands alone on its side; the parts join together.

facts.title: The inverse opens the box
facts.explanation: Undo the addition with a subtraction — then substitute to check.

workedExamples.statement: Write the four facts of the family $53$, $38$, $91$.
workedExamples.solution: $53 + 38 = 91$ and $38 + 53 = 91$; $91 - 38 = 53$ and $91 - 53 = 38$. The whole ($91$) always stands alone on one side of the equals sign.

workedExamples.note: The box was cut by 47 and still shows 129 — it started bigger.
workedExamples.solution: Undo the cut with addition: $\square = 129 + 47 = 176$. Substitute: $176 - 47 = 129$ ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Adding whatever two numbers appear — solving □ + 38 = 91 as 91 + 38 = 129.
commonMistakes.correction: The box and 38 TOGETHER make 91, so the box is smaller than 91: undo with 91 − 38 = 53, and substitute: 53 + 38 = 91 ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Subtracting on □ − 47 = 129 because the equation shows a minus sign.
commonMistakes.correction: The box LOST 47 and still has 129 — it started bigger: □ = 129 + 47 = 176. Undo what the equation DID, not what its sign looks like.

tryIt.statement: Write the four facts of the family $160$, $340$, $500$.

steps.title: Three numbers, four facts
beats: Put the three numbers on a triangle: the whole $91$ on top, the parts $53$ and $38$ below. That one triangle holds FOUR facts.
Adding reads it upward — $53 + 38 = 91$ and $38 + 53 = 91$. Subtracting reads it downward — $91 - 38 = 53$ and $91 - 53 = 38$.
Cover any corner and the other two rebuild it. That is the secret of this whole lesson: addition and subtraction are ONE fact read in different directions.

steps.title: Four outfits
steps.intro: The whole on top, parts below — four readings.

examples.prompt: The family of $285$, $460$, $745$ — write its two subtractions.

steps.title: Family members only
steps.intro: The whole stands alone; the parts join.

problems.prompt: Which fact belongs to the family of $27$, $45$, $72$?
problems.explanation: The whole $72$ stands alone: $72 - 45 = 27$ ✓ (receipt $27 + 45 = 72$). The other two drag in strangers — $18$ and $99$ are not family members.

problems.prompt: In the family of $160$, $340$, $500$, one subtraction fact is:
problems.explanation: The whole $500$ gives up a part: $500 - 160 = 340$ ✓ (receipt $340 + 160 = 500$). The middle claim misses: $500 - 340 = 160$, not $260$. And $340 - 160$ could never GROW to $500$.

problems.prompt: Two members of a family are $250$ and $480$, with $480$ the whole. The third member is:
problems.explanation: Part = whole minus part: $480 - 250 = 230$, receipted by $230 + 250 = 480$ ✓. $730$ ADDED the two — but a part can never outgrow its whole.

steps.title: Count the outfits
steps.prompt: How many facts does the family $16$, $59$, $75$ hold?
options: four — two additions and two subtractions
steps.explanation: $16 + 59 = 75$, $59 + 16 = 75$, $75 - 59 = 16$, $75 - 16 = 59$: four faces of one fact. Learn one triangle, own four equations.

steps.title: Two little lines
steps.body: The $=$ sign was invented in the 1500s by Robert Recorde, a Welsh mathematician. He chose a pair of parallel lines of one length because, he wrote, no two things can be more equal. Every fact family you write balances on his little invention.

steps.title: Boxes opened by the inverse
beats: $\square + 38 = 91$ is a family with one corner hidden. Do not guess — the INVERSE digs it out: subtraction undoes addition, so $\square = 91 - 38 = 53$.
When the box was cut, addition restores it: $\square - 47 = 129$ means the box LOST $47$ and still shows $129$ — so $\square = 129 + 47 = 176$. Read what happened to the box, then do the opposite.
Always SUBSTITUTE the answer back: $53 + 38 = 91$ ✓ and $176 - 47 = 129$ ✓. Substitution is the receipt in its smartest clothes.

steps.title: Undo, then substitute
steps.intro: Read what happened to the box; do the opposite.

steps: The box gained $38$; take it away: $\square = 91 - 38 = 53$. Counting up agrees: $38$ to $40$ is $2$, to $90$ is $50$ more, to $91$ is $1$ more — $2 + 50 + 1 = 53$.
$620$ lost the box and kept $265$ — so the box and $265$ are the two parts of $620$: $\square = 620 - 265 = 355$.

steps.title: Open the box
steps.intro: Inverse first, substitution always.

problems.explanation: Undo the added $260$: $730 - 260 = 470$; substitute $470 + 260 = 730$ ✓. $990$ ADDED instead ($730 + 260$) — but a box that gains $260$ to reach $730$ must start below $730$.
The box lost $155$ and kept $245$: restore it — $245 + 155 = 400$; substitute $400 - 155 = 245$ ✓. $90$ comes from $245 - 155$ — undoing in the wrong direction.
The box and $386$ are the two parts of $1\,000$: $\square = 1\,000 - 386 = 614$; substitute $1\,000 - 614 = 386$ ✓.

steps.title: Substitution catches it
steps.prompt: $\square - 84 = 312$. Otgo answers $228$, from computing $312 - 84$. What does substitution say?
steps.explanation: Put the offer back: $228 - 84 = 144$, not $312$ — rejected. The box LOST $84$, so restore by adding: $312 + 84 = 396$, and indeed $396 - 84 = 312$ ✓. The minus sign in the equation does not mean YOU subtract — undo what the equation did.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Three numbers, four facts: two additions, two subtractions — one triangle.
The whole stands alone on its side; parts join together.
Open a box with the inverse: undo what the equation DID to it.
Substitute every answer back — a wrong box fails its own equation.
Addition and subtraction are one fact read two ways: that is the whole machinery.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: For each box, first say aloud what happened to it — 'the box gained 260', 'the box lost 155' — then do the opposite, and substitute to sign the receipt.

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Families and boxes, receipts throughout.

problems.prompt: Which addition belongs to the family $125$, $375$, $500$?
problems.explanation: Parts join to make the whole: $125 + 375 = 500$ ✓. The others add the whole itself to a part, making the strangers $625$ and $875$.
$900 - 476 = 424$; substitute $424 + 476 = 900$ ✓. $1\,376$ added the two numbers.
The box lost $238$: restore it — $517 + 238 = 755$; substitute $755 - 238 = 517$ ✓. $279$ subtracted instead ($517 - 238$).
The box and $447$ are the parts of $903$: $903 - 447 = 456$; substitute $903 - 456 = 447$ ✓. $1\,350$ added.

problems.prompt: Saruul had some togrog saved. She spent $350$ on a hair clip and has $480$ left. How much did she start with?
problems.explanation: The story is a box equation: $\square - 350 = 480$. Restore: $480 + 350 = 830$; substitute $830 - 350 = 480$ ✓. $130$ subtracted the story's numbers — but spending REDUCED her savings, so the start must be the biggest number of the three.

steps.title: You've finished "Missing Numbers"
steps.body: Fact families gave you the inverse; boxes taught substitution. Last lesson: stories — where the numbers arrive dressed as sheep, togrog and Naadam tickets, and YOU choose the operation.

lessons.title: Word Problems
lessons.concreteComparison: Two questions about the same pen of animals: 'how many altogether?' wants the flocks JOINED — addition; 'how many more sheep than goats?' wants the gap measured — subtraction. The numbers are identical; the STORY picks the operation. Reading the story's shape is the real work; the arithmetic afterwards is last week's job.
lessons.objective: Solve one- and two-step word problems inside 10 000 — reading the story's shape to choose addition or subtraction, finding hidden numbers first, and receipting every answer.
concept: **The story picks the operation.** Joining shapes — altogether, in all, total, gained, more arrive — ADD. Gap shapes — how many more X than Y, how many fewer X than Y, how many left — SUBTRACT. One word decides nothing: 'more' joins in '$29$ more arrive' and measures a gap in 'how many more sheep than goats'. Read the whole question sentence.

**Two-step stories hide a number.** 'Spent $1\,250$ and then $850$ out of $3\,600$' hides the TOTAL SPENT: find it first ($2\,100$), then answer the real question ($3\,600 - 2\,100 = 1\,500$). Name the hidden number before touching any arithmetic.

**Every answer carries a receipt.** One step or two: add the answer back, or walk the other road — $3\,600 - 1\,250 - 850$ lands on the same $1\,500$. Two roads agreeing is the strongest receipt there is.
lessons.keyIdea: Read the story's shape, find the hidden number first, and receipt every answer — two roads to the same number make it true.

facts.title: Story shapes
facts.latex: \text{altogether, in all} \to + \qquad \text{how many more X than Y, how many left} \to -
facts.explanation: Joining stories add; gap and taking-away stories subtract. The word 'more' on its own is NOT a subtraction signal — '29 more arrive' joins.

facts.title: Two steps, one receipt
facts.explanation: Find the hidden total first; then receipt: 1500 + 2100 rebuilds 3600.

workedExamples.statement: A herder's flock holds $1\,250$ sheep and $860$ goats. How many animals altogether?
workedExamples.solution: Join the flocks: $1\,250 + 860 = 2\,110$ animals. Other-way check: $860 + 1\,250 = 2\,110$ ✓.

workedExamples.statement: Bilguun saves $3\,600$ togrog. At the market he buys a notebook for $1\,250$ and a pen for $850$. How much is left?
workedExamples.note: Two steps — the total cost is hidden.
workedExamples.solution: Hidden number, the total cost: $1\,250 + 850 = 2\,100$. Then $3\,600 - 2\,100 = 1\,500$ togrog left. Receipts: $1\,500 + 2\,100 = 3\,600$ ✓, and the second road $3\,600 - 1\,250 - 850 = 1\,500$ agrees ✓.

commonMistakes.text: Grabbing the two numbers and adding, whatever the question asks.
commonMistakes.correction: The STORY chooses the operation: joining shapes add; 'how many more X than Y' and 'how many left' subtract. Read the question sentence twice before touching the numbers — 'more' on its own can join ('29 more arrive') or measure a gap.

commonMistakes.text: Stopping after step one of a two-step problem.
commonMistakes.correction: Ask: does my number answer THE question, or a stepping-stone question? 380 + 295 = 675 khuushuur SOLD is the stepping stone; 850 − 675 = 175 LEFT answers the question.

tryIt.statement: At the wrestling, $875$ spectators are watching; $390$ leave for the horse race. How many stay? Receipt your answer.
tryIt.solution: A leaving shape subtracts: $875 - 390 = 485$ stay. Receipt: $485 + 390 = 875$ ✓.

tryIt.statement: A library holds $1\,480$ books. It receives $260$ new ones, then lends out $575$. How many are on the shelves?

steps.title: Read the story's shape
beats: By the ger graze $8$ sheep and $5$ goats. 'How many animals ALTOGETHER?' joins the groups: $8 + 5 = 13$. Joining words — altogether, in all, total, gained — always add.

Same animals, different question: 'how many MORE sheep THAN goats?' measures the gap: $8 - 5 = 3$. Gap phrases — 'how many more X than Y', 'how many fewer X than Y', 'how many left', 'how many remain' — subtract.
Watch out for the word 'more' on its own: it can JOIN instead. '$29$ more guests arrive' adds. Only the whole phrase 'how many more X THAN Y' asks for a gap — so read the phrase, never one word.
The numbers never choose the operation; the story's SHAPE does. Read the question sentence twice, name the shape, then compute — and receipt: $3 + 5 = 8$ ✓.

steps.title: One-step stories
steps.intro: Name the shape first; compute second; receipt third.

examples.prompt: $1\,250$ sheep and $860$ goats — how many animals altogether?
$875$ spectators are watching the wrestling; $390$ leave. How many stay?

steps.title: Joining or gap?
steps.intro: The question sentence decides.

problems.prompt: By the river graze $14$ sheep and $9$ goats. How many animals altogether?
problems.explanation: Altogether joins: $14 + 9 = 23$. Answering $5$ measured the gap ($14 - 9 = 5$, since $5 + 9 = 14$) — the wrong shape for this question.

problems.prompt: A school has $468$ girls and $415$ boys. How many MORE girls than boys?
problems.explanation: 'How many more' is a gap: $468 - 415 = 53$, receipted by $53 + 415 = 468$ ✓. $883$ joined the groups — the altogether answer to a gap question.

problems.prompt: $2\,500$ Naadam tickets were printed and $1\,730$ sold. How many are unsold?
problems.explanation: Unsold is what is LEFT: $2\,500 - 1\,730 = 770$, receipted by $770 + 1\,730 = 2\,500$ ✓. $4\,230$ added the story's numbers.

steps.title: Spot the shape
options: Tuya had $900$ togrog and spent $350$ — how much is left?
A pen holds $12$ sheep and $8$ goats — how many animals in all?
Bat read $365$ pages last month and $120$ this month — how many altogether?
A herd of $56$ horses gains $40$ foals — how big is it now?
steps.explanation: 'Spent, and how much is LEFT' takes away: $900 - 350 = 550$, receipt $550 + 350 = 900$ ✓. The other three all JOIN amounts: $12 + 8 = 20$, $365 + 120 = 485$, $56 + 40 = 96$.

steps.title: The three games of Naadam
steps.body: Naadam, Mongolia's great summer festival, centres on three sports: wrestling, horse racing and archery. The long-distance horse races are ridden by child jockeys across open steppe rather than around a track. And the stands are full of arithmetic — scores, distances and ticket counts all day long.

steps.title: Two-step stories
beats: Some stories will not solve in one move: 'Bilguun has $3\,600$ togrog and buys a notebook for $1\,250$ and a pen for $850$ — how much is left?' The cost of BOTH things is hidden. Name it, then find it: $1\,250 + 850 = 2\,100$.
Now the real question is one step: $3\,600 - 2\,100 = 1\,500$ togrog left. Step one finds the hidden number; step two answers the question.

Receipt with two roads: subtracting the prices one at a time — $3\,600 - 1\,250 = 2\,350$, then $2\,350 - 850 = 1\,500$ — lands on the same answer. Two roads agreeing is the strongest receipt there is.

steps.title: Hidden numbers
steps.intro: Find what the story hides; then answer what it asks.

examples.prompt: Bilguun has $3\,600$ togrog and buys a notebook for $1\,250$ and a pen for $850$. How much is left?
A library holds $1\,480$ books; $260$ new ones arrive, then $575$ are lent out. How many remain?

steps.title: Two moves, one answer
steps.intro: Name the hidden number before you compute.

problems.prompt: A bus carries $46$ passengers. At the market $18$ get off and $11$ get on. How many ride now?
problems.explanation: Two steps: $46 - 18 = 28$ (receipt $28 + 18 = 46$ ✓), then $28 + 11 = 39$. $75$ added everything; $17$ subtracted everything — each ignored half the story.

problems.prompt: A camp kitchen fried $850$ khuushuur, selling $380$ in the morning and $295$ in the afternoon. How many are left?
problems.explanation: Hidden number — total sold: $380 + 295 = 675$. Left: $850 - 675 = 175$, receipted by $175 + 675 = 850$ ✓. $675$ stops at step one.

problems.prompt: Bat picks $145$ sea buckthorn berries and his sister picks $168$. They eat $96$. How many berries remain?

steps.title: Finish the story
steps.prompt: In the khuushuur story, Zaya answers $675$. What happened?
options: she stopped at step one — $675$ is the amount SOLD, but the question asks what is LEFT: $850 - 675 = 175$
she should have added the $850$ as well
the story cannot be solved without more information
steps.explanation: Step one's result answers a stepping-stone question, not the story's question. Re-read the final sentence: LEFT means subtract the sold total from $850$ — $175$, receipted by $175 + 675 = 850$ ✓.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Joining shapes (altogether, in all, gained, more arrive) add; gap shapes (how many more X than Y, how many fewer X than Y, how many left) subtract.
The numbers never pick the operation — the question sentence does. 'More' by itself decides nothing: read the whole phrase.
Two-step stories hide a number: name it, find it, THEN answer the question.
Receipt every answer — add it back, or walk the second road and watch the answers agree.
An answer without a receipt is an offer, not a fact.

steps.title: Time to practice
steps.body: Underline the question sentence, say the shape aloud, and after computing ask: did I answer THE question, or a stepping stone?

steps.title: Mixed practice
steps.intro: Stories of every shape, receipts on every answer.

problems.prompt: $1\,675$ adults and $980$ children watched the horse race finish. How many spectators altogether?
problems.explanation: Joining shape: $1\,675 + 980 = 2\,655$, and the other way $980 + 1\,675$ agrees ✓. $695$ measured the gap ($1\,675 - 980 = 695$, since $695 + 980 = 1\,675$).

problems.prompt: A book costs $3\,250$ togrog; Oyun pays with a $5\,000$ note. Her change is:
problems.explanation: Change is what is left of the note: $5\,000 - 3\,250 = 1\,750$, receipted the cashier's way: $1\,750 + 3\,250 = 5\,000$ ✓. $8\,250$ added the price to the note.

problems.prompt: A shelf holds $248$ books; $67$ are borrowed, then $35$ returned books come back. How many stand on the shelf?
problems.explanation: $248 - 67 = 181$ (receipt $181 + 67 = 248$ ✓), then $181 + 35 = 216$. $146$ subtracted both numbers; $350$ added both.

problems.prompt: Sarnai's book has $900$ pages. She reads $356$ pages one week and $288$ the next. How many pages are left?
problems.explanation: Hidden number — pages read: $356 + 288 = 644$. Left: $900 - 644 = 256$, receipted by $256 + 644 = 900$ ✓. $644$ stops at step one.

problems.prompt: The ger camp had $78$ guests; $29$ more arrive for Naadam. Which operation, and how many now?
problems.explanation: Arriving guests JOIN: $78 + 29 = 107$ (make-ten: $78 + 2 = 80$, then $80 + 27 = 107$). Here 'more' means 'more arrive', a joining word — the gap phrase would be 'how many MORE guests THAN yesterday'. So the subtraction $78 - 29 = 49$ reads the story backwards; $97$ drops the carry.

steps.title: You've finished "Word Problems" — and the whole topic
steps.body: Column addition, column subtraction, mental shortcuts, fact families, and stories: five lessons circling one idea — addition and subtraction are one fact read two ways, so every answer can sign its own receipt. Multiplication picks up the story from here.

practice.statement: Compute $476 + 358$ in columns, then check by adding the other way.
Compute $904 - 568$, showing the regrouped outfit of $904$ first.
Compute $456 + 399$ in your head, with compensation.
practice.solution: Overshoot: $456 + 400 = 856$; give the extra $1$ back: $855$ (and $855 + 1 = 856$ confirms the settle). So $456 + 399 = 855$.
The box lost $260$: restore it — $480 + 260 = 740$. Substitute: $740 - 260 = 480$ ✓.

practice.statement: $1\,265$ adults and $985$ children watched the archery at Naadam. How many spectators altogether?
Tuya brings $5\,000$ togrog to the bookshop and buys a book for $2\,350$ and a pencil case for $1\,425$. How much does she carry home?

testYourself.statement: Compute $2\,486 + 3\,957$, checked by adding the other way.
Compute in your head, naming the strategy: $647 + 99$, then $835 - 97$.
testYourself.solution: Compensation both times. $647 + 100 = 747$, give $1$ back: $746$. And $835 - 100 = 735$ took $3$ too many, so give them back: $735 + 3 = 738$. Receipt: $738 + 97 = 835$ ✓.

testYourself.statement: Write the four facts of the family $245$, $380$, $625$.
A herd of $2\,400$ animals holds $1\,350$ sheep; the rest are goats. After $275$ goats are sold, how many goats remain?
